[h1]
Who play this? Seriously.
[/h1]

Mainlining is a cyberpunk-inspired investigative adventure that turns the ordinary process of browsing files, reading emails, and searching databases into a tense and immersive detective experience. Developed by Rebelephant and published by Merge Games, the game places players behind the screen of a government intelligence computer system where every clue, suspect, and secret must be uncovered through hacking, surveillance, and careful analysis of digital information. Instead of relying on action sequences or cinematic set pieces, Mainlining builds suspense entirely through deduction, atmosphere, and the unsettling realization that every citizen’s private life is only a few clicks away from exposure.

The game is set in a near-future Britain where privacy laws have collapsed following the introduction of the BLU Pill Act, legislation that grants intelligence agencies unrestricted access to personal digital information. Players take on the role of an operative working for MI7, a government surveillance division tasked with tracking cybercriminals after a major breach compromises national security. What initially appears to be a series of disconnected investigations slowly evolves into a larger conspiracy involving corruption, abuse of power, political manipulation, and the dangers of mass surveillance. The story feels particularly effective because its themes mirror real-world debates surrounding government monitoring and digital privacy, giving the experience a level of relevance that extends beyond simple science fiction.

One of Mainlining’s greatest achievements is its presentation. The entire game takes place inside a simulated retro computer operating system inspired by older versions of Windows desktops. Every action occurs through email clients, command prompts, browsers, folders, chat programs, and intelligence databases, creating the illusion that the player is genuinely operating inside a classified surveillance network. This design choice immediately establishes immersion because players interact with the world exactly the way an investigator would. The retro-inspired pixel art and low-tech interface also contribute heavily to the atmosphere, giving the game a gritty and believable cyberpunk identity without relying on flashy visuals.

Gameplay revolves around investigating suspects by hacking into personal computers and analyzing digital traces left behind in their online activity. Players search through conversations, photographs, browsing histories, financial records, and social media interactions in order to uncover evidence and identify criminal behavior. Unlike many detective games that heavily guide the player toward obvious solutions, Mainlining encourages independent thinking and observation. Important clues are often hidden within seemingly unimportant files or casual conversations, forcing players to pay close attention to details instead of simply following objective markers.

The command-line hacking mechanics are surprisingly immersive despite their simplicity. Players use text commands to access networks, trace IP addresses, and infiltrate systems, creating the feeling of performing real investigative work without becoming inaccessible to newcomers. The game succeeds because it understands how to make information itself feel rewarding. Discovering a hidden message, uncovering an encrypted file, or linking multiple suspects together creates genuine excitement because progress depends entirely on the player’s own deductions rather than scripted sequences.

What truly separates Mainlining from other hacking-themed games is the moral discomfort that develops over time. Although the player technically works for law enforcement, many of the investigative methods feel invasive and ethically questionable. Reading intimate personal conversations, examining private photographs, and monitoring every aspect of someone’s digital life creates a constant sense of unease. The game repeatedly raises questions about whether unrestricted surveillance can ever remain justified once governments gain the ability to observe every citizen without limitations. Even when tracking criminals, the player often feels disturbingly close to violating the boundaries of innocent people.

The investigations themselves remain varied enough to keep the campaign engaging. Cases involve cybercrime, hacking groups, drug operations, financial fraud, and organized conspiracies that slowly reveal deeper connections hidden beneath the surface. Players must carefully identify suspects, gather evidence, and determine physical locations before making arrests. Wrong accusations can result in failure, adding pressure to every investigation and encouraging players to double-check conclusions before acting. This structure creates a satisfying detective experience because success feels earned through careful reasoning rather than random guessing.

The writing throughout the game is consistently strong. Dialogue balances serious political themes with dry humor and believable character interactions that prevent the experience from becoming overly bleak. Emails, online chats, and casual conversations reveal small personality details that make suspects and supporting characters feel authentic despite the minimalist presentation. The game gradually builds a believable world where political fear, digital dependence, and government overreach have become deeply intertwined with everyday life.

The soundtrack complements the atmosphere exceptionally well. Electronic music and ambient background tracks create a constant feeling of tension and paranoia without overwhelming the quieter investigative moments. Combined with the glowing retro desktop aesthetic and endless streams of digital information, the audio design reinforces the sense that players are trapped inside a cold and impersonal surveillance system.

Despite its originality, Mainlining is not completely free from flaws. Some investigations can become repetitive because the gameplay loop often revolves around similar patterns of searching files and tracing connections. Certain clues are occasionally too obscure, leading to moments where progression slows due to unclear objectives. The command-line interface, while immersive, can also feel awkward at times because typing errors or unclear system responses occasionally interrupt the pacing. Players expecting action-heavy hacking gameplay may also find the experience too slow because most of the tension comes from reading, analyzing information, and making logical deductions rather than participating in high-energy sequences.

The visual presentation, while stylish, is intentionally minimalistic and may not appeal to everyone. Those expecting large cinematic environments or highly animated storytelling may initially find the desktop-only structure limiting. However, the simplicity ultimately becomes one of the game’s strengths because it keeps the player fully focused on the investigation itself rather than external distractions.

Although it lacks major production values or complex action mechanics, Mainlining stands out as one of the more memorable indie hacking adventures available. Its investigative gameplay, morally ambiguous storytelling, and immersive interface design create a unique experience that rewards patience, observation, and curiosity. Players interested in conspiracy thrillers, cybercrime investigations, and narrative-driven puzzle games will likely find themselves completely absorbed by its dark digital world.

Instead of repeating what other people have already said, let me first point you to two well-written negative reviews that pinpoint exactly what made the gameplay kind of a chore:

https://steamcommunity.com/id/algorithman/recommended/454950/

https://steamcommunity.com/id/Oloko0/recommended/454950/

In addition to that, the concept of the missions is sometimes weird. Every mission ends by arresting a single suspect. Sometimes you just have 1 suspect, sometimes there are 3 possible suspects and you just have to arrest any of them, not all 3. That's also the case in a mission where you're just told to find information on a person who went missing years ago. You can randomly find information on her ex-husband, arrest him for producing drugs with her, and you win. And the game just never even follows up on that, except in the credits where you suddenly find out that the missing person is dead.

There's other weird stuff going on like a puzzle in the final mission where you need to find the suspect's son's first name, and in the ending, he suddenly has a different name. I also found a placeholder document that said something like "Following the suspect's arrest on [date the player arrested him]"

Summary: The story was pretty good, and has other things going for it, but it feels really unpolished, poor UI, typos etc.

Things I did like: The story was engaging, and the writers did a good job in making their points about government surveillance. The core hacking gameplay is also good (albeit not very realistic but this is at least explained in game). They did a good job theming the OSes.

Things I didn't like: The UI is not good, I get that they aren't going to recode in a whole desktop environment, but you can't resize windows, text files that are opened cannot be minimized nor do they show up in the taskbar. This makes windows all overlap in an annoying way. The other thing I didn't like is the lack of continuity between cases. Changing the IP addresses each case is annoying. The fact I couldn't take more than like 256 characters of notes in the notepad app is also annoying. You can't move your cursor back to insert something into text, you have to delete it and start over.

Its weird the game's narrative and the story cases all link together but the gamestate basically wipes at each case. For example I would have liked to keep a list of websites I visited, as well as persons of interest and details about each. But because the notes are all deleted from case to case (in fact they are deleted as soon as you close the notepad app). It makes that pointless. Files are the same way, all your downloaded files are deleted from case to case. Sometimes in a detective game its useful to go back to reference old info, even if its not immediately useful for solving the case. I just felt that the game's mechanics kept holding me back from being fully immersed in the game.

There are also alot of typos. Some of which are in important places.

The way you turn in cases is also kinda clunky. Its a good idea but it ends up being frustrated on several cases. There is also not any rewards or effects on the story for getting the highest rating for cases.

Honestly I wanted to like this, but there's just too many irritating bad things about everything from story to design. It takes place in a city so fictional that it's hard to care about it - it exists only because it needs to have a game be set in it. From the technology perspective nothing makes sense. Especially if you work in anything related to IT, it will simply make you cringe. You hack into people's computers simply by finding their IP address... It's like you're living inside a meme. The interface tries to resemble Windows XP for some reason... Even though the game is very low res pixelated, which makes no sense. Nothing is visually pleasant or cool to interact with. Everything inside is barely functional jank, like the notepad that doesn't let you save files or move the cursor into previously entered lines. Honestly, Steam's notes or even pen & paper are more useful, so it's hard to say why this exists. The method of investigating cases is repetitive and boring and a lot has to be based on guesswork, detaching the game from it's intelligence gathering theme. Even worse is how you solve them, which is simply a blind test that you can repeat infinitely until you get all the elements right. It's just disappointing, after playing Uplink and Hypnospace Outlaw there's really nothing that would make me consider going back to Mainlining even for a moment.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Mainlining is a police investigation drama that plays out through the retro style Windows XP desktop of your cyber crimes computer. You pursue criminals and hackers by following leads to websites, hacking into computers, and collecting evidence to make arrests.

The gameplay has you using a faux desktop complete with web browser, downloading files, and using the police instant messenger to coordinate with the other agents (all scripted of course). Arresting a criminal requires several key pieces of information which you can gather through hacking websites and investigating the contents. The game can be a little buggy but has some interesting ideas and the usual twists as you follow the investigation with the stakes constantly getting raised. The story isn't doing anything new and follows the usual tropes but it's a fun ride.

I'm a fan of these hacking simulator games, and playing as a 'good guy' was a nice change of pace. Plus the episode to episode gameplay loop is fun with the desktop graphics and art being a nice change of pace compared to the command line gimmicks every other hacking game wants to employ.

Overall a fun game that doesn't really push the envelope, but its good for one play through if you're into the hacking puzzle genre.

Mainlining is a satirical dystopian hacking adventure where you are the law... The fictional MI-7 in a future where unlicensed software development carries at 25-year jail sentence. Your job as a MI-7 agent is to hack your way across the map, chase down suspects, hack their machines for evidence, then issue arrest warrants which must include their location (which district) as well as what evidence do you offer as evidence of their crime (obtained legally... or not). 

The game pokes fun at current practices as there are callouts of all the major OSs and their UI quirks. The default, Rainbow OS, is clearly Windows, but you'll also find analog for MacOS, Linux, and even Chrome OS. There are also callouts to the various web browsers, major apps like Dropbox (Skybox here), and even live wallpapers. There's also AirTag, IRC, PGP, and so on. And of course, the good ol' command prompt. 

What's interesting is there's often more than one way to solve a case. Generally, the case just needs ONE arrest, but often, you may find several pieces of evidence that lets you chose who to arrest and what for (what evidence to convict them with). 

Not much replay value, but it is fun while it lasts.

+ Pretty art
+ cool concept and UI

- Buggy and not optimized.
- Story and choices you're supposed to make (accusations) dont make sense sometimes/aren't clear. Even a user who created a guide walkthrough wrongly wrote who to accuse to progress the game because of this (and later edited).

- lots of text mistakes like names of another character at the end of a sentence of an article that has nothing to do with them (im choosing to not be nitpicky because there are bigger issues but I will mention there is inconsistencies with text usernames and repetitive words which I assume are human error and I can look past that but there are quite a few)

- hard to keep track of story more particularly when you take breaks from each case. I wish there was some sort of followup or briefing folder to look back on after wrapping up each case, especially for important notes. Mainlining is a story-driven hacking-flavoured thriller/adventure game with gameplay closer to a point-and-click adventure than than the "Hollywood" hackers (Uplink, etc).

Set in a slightly dystopian near future, you are an MI7 agent empowered to hack into citizen's computers to prevent cybercrime.  Each chapter presents the player with a new crime to solve by finding IPs, connecting to them, downloading documents, and following the trail until you can apply for an arrest warrant.

Graphics and sound are all serviceable, characters dialogue are charming, and the developers put a lot of time into huge suspect database, variety of interfaces, and multiple solutions to each chapter.

Mainlining is solid game from a small indie team, but does lack polish in a few areas. A number of websites that should exist in the game do not, there are numerous spelling errors and several "Welcome, $USERNAME" type bugs, and the in-game tools have a lot of minor UX issues that can be frustrating.  In particular, the warrant system is somewhat notorious for being too exacting, but the cost of failure is low, so it is tolerable.

Overall definitely worth a playthough if you like the demo.

I liked Mainlining at first, because I like the visual style and it also has a backstory (unlike most other "hacking" games).
I would forgive the bad UX of the command prompt and the incompleteness of the universe (e.g. websites only exist for the time of the missions in which they appear) and some other minor issues.

But the dealbreaker for me is how stupid the missions are. You have to identify perpetrators, collect evidence against them and find their whereabouts. Okay - that COULD be fun. But a huge part of the problem is that - when you get one of the ingredients wrong, you get no useful information on WHICH ingredient was wrong. If the location isn't correct, then why does the newspaper say that the suspect had been "wrongly accused" and "released"? This phrasing indicates that the location was right but the evidence to weak. Okay - so the feedback is misleading and (once you have figured THAT out!) you have to look at the clues and logically deduce the ingredients. Right? That would constitute a PUZZLE-game. That would make sense. That would be fun. But that's not how Mainlining rolls.

Oftentimes you have to submit a piece of evidence that would never hold up in court - even when you have collected much better evidence that isn't accepted. Also you often have evidence against multiple suspects. So you are already guessing between 6 to 30 combinations of these two ingredients. As to the whereabouts: you have access to everybodys addresses, but usually there is a vague hint to a different location in one of the files - and I mean VAGUE. And if there isn't such a hint, you are still always in doubt whether you have overlooked one. AND ON TOP OF THAT there are sometimes twists that require leaps in your reasoning that only make sense in hindsight. Mission 7 in particular was so harebrained that I FURIOUSLY uninstalled the game after reading that insult of a "solution" in a walkthrough.

I'm convinced that Rebelephant wasted to much time on side-gimmicks like the "maps" view, ran out of time in development and could only design a handful of missions, so they deliberately made the solutions illogical to artificially extend the playing-time. Illogical puzzle games aren't fun, they are frustrating. VERY FRUSTRATING. So although I really want to like this game - I can only advise you to STAY AWAY from it!

Mainlining is one of the few games to follow in the footsteps of Uplink, and occupies a sweet spot between its predecessors’ “hacking-as-puzzle” focus and a traditional graphic adventure. I have been teetering on the recommendation for Mainlining for quite a while, and I think I'd recommend this game only to fans of detective and/or hacking sims, or if you can grab it on a sale. 

The game features good art, great music and I really enjoyed the pixelated re-imagination of multiple operating-systems, albeit the pixel-fonts are a little hard to read at times. 
Generally speaking, I think Mainlining is more of a detective than hacking simulation. The hacking aspect is relatively simplistic and the game's limited command line turns hacking into a bit of a chore, i.e. you are required to type the same set of commands over and over for every new case and history or tab-completion isn't supported. At least, you are able to abbreviate most commands to their initial, e.g. "a", instead of typing out the entire commend. I find it puzzling, that possibility of abbreviating commands (that doesn't exist in a RL command line) wasn't communicated in the game itself, rather I stumbled upon this in a video-review. Nonetheless, I did enjoy playing this game at a virtual computer screen, and each case created enough suspension to keep me interested until the ending credits rolled.

While I have fond memories of the OS environments, my overall enjoyment of the game got hampered by frequent and annoying bugs as well as seemingly careless typos. Furthermore, these issues increase in frequency and the game is noticeably decreasing in quality in the latter half.
